nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the autocrat, the physician and the occasional poet
literary_identity: Physician, poet and essayist; the author of The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table and one of the founders of the Atlantic Monthly.
biography: Born in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on 29 August 1809; he studied medicine in Paris, taught anatomy at Harvard, and made his literary name with The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table (1858). The Professor at the Breakfast-Table (1860), The Poet at the Breakfast-Table (1872), Elsie Venner (1861) and many occasional poems followed. He died in Boston on 7 October 1894.
literary_profile: Holmes was the finest conversational essayist in American literature and the founder of the Atlantic Monthly's style: The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table created the American familiar essay, and his medical novels made the case study into fiction and anticipated the psychological novel.
stylistic_characteristics: The discursive table-talk of the breakfast room; the epigram and the pun; the medical case study folded into narrative; the occasional poem written to order; the urbane, witty, self-mocking prose of the Boston man of letters.
intellectual_concerns: Science, religion, and the question of design; the city of Boston and its elite; education and the cultivation of the self; heredity and the medical body; death and the consolation of wit.
historical_significance: Oliver Wendell Holmes was the finest conversational essayist in American literature and the founder of the Atlantic Monthly's style: The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table created the American familiar essay and his medical novels made the case study into fiction.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the satirist, the critic and the man of letters
literary_identity: Poet, critic, editor and diplomat; the first editor of the Atlantic Monthly and one of the central figures of the American Renaissance.
biography: Born in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on 22 February 1819; he made his name with the Biglow Papers (1848), the Yankee dialect satire on the Mexican War, and A Fable for Critics (1848). He edited the Atlantic Monthly from 1857 and the North American Review from 1864, and was American minister in Madrid and London from 1877 to 1885. He died in Cambridge on 12 August 1891.
literary_profile: Lowell was the most versatile man of letters in nineteenth-century America and the first editor of the Atlantic Monthly: the Biglow Papers created the American political satire in dialect, A Fable for Critics invented the verse review of contemporaries, and his criticism made the transatlantic reputation of American letters.
stylistic_characteristics: The Yankee dialect of Hosea Biglow; the verse satire and the parody; the critical essay and the review; the public ode in the classical manner; the pun and the learned joke.
intellectual_concerns: Slavery and the Mexican War; democracy and the American experiment; the vocation of letters; the transatlantic relation of America and Europe; education and the New England tradition.
historical_significance: James Russell Lowell was the most versatile man of letters in nineteenth-century America and the first editor of the Atlantic Monthly: the Biglow Papers created the American political satire in dialect, and A Fable for Critics invented the verse review of contemporaries.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the magazine sketch and the society letter
literary_identity: Poet, editor and magazine writer; the most popular magazine writer in America in the 1840s and the inventor of the American society column.
biography: Born in Portland, Maine, on 20 January 1806; he travelled in Europe as a foreign correspondent, edited the American Monthly Magazine and the New York Mirror, and made his fortune with the Home Journal from 1846. His Sketches (1835), Letters from Under a Bridge (1840) and Out-Doors at Idlewild (1855) were widely read. He died at Idlewild, his estate on the Hudson, on 20 January 1867.
literary_profile: Willis was the most popular magazine writer in America in the 1840s and the inventor of the American society column: his sketches of London and Paris society, his country-house letters and his gossip made the personal essay into a mass-market form and prepared the way for the American magazine of the later century.
stylistic_characteristics: The familiar letter from abroad; the social sketch and the celebrity interview; the description of the great house and the fashionable assembly; the light, confiding, confidential tone; the sentiment of the home circle.
intellectual_concerns: The metropolis and fashionable society; travel and the transatlantic comparison; the home and the domestic affections; money and the literary marketplace; the American scene as spectacle.
historical_significance: N. P. Willis was the most popular magazine writer in America in the 1840s and the inventor of the American society column: his sketches and letters made the personal essay into a mass-market form and created the readership for the American magazine.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the ecstatic sonnet and the transcendentalist crisis
literary_identity: Poet and essayist; the most intense of the transcendentalist poets and the author of a body of visionary sonnets written during a single year of crisis.
biography: Born in Salem, Massachusetts, on 28 August 1813; he studied at Harvard Divinity School, where in 1838 he experienced a religious crisis, announced that he was the Holy Spirit, and was briefly confined to an asylum. Emerson published his Essays and Poems in 1839. He spent the rest of his life as a private tutor and died in Salem on 8 May 1880.
literary_profile: Jones Very wrote the most intense visionary poetry of the American transcendentalist movement: the sonnets of 1838, written in a single year of religious crisis and published by Emerson, are the purest American expression of the ecstatic, and they gave the transcendentalist movement its martyr and its most original poet.
stylistic_characteristics: The sonnet as ecstatic utterance; the short declarative line; the paradox and the riddle of divine indwelling; the absence of ornament; the prophetic first person.
intellectual_concerns: Divine indwelling and the Holy Spirit; the annihilation of the self in God; nature as the language of spirit; death and the soul; the transcendentalist crisis of the will.
historical_significance: Jones Very wrote the most intense visionary poetry of the American transcendentalist movement: his 1838 sonnets, published by Emerson, are the purest American expression of the ecstatic and gave transcendentalism its most original poet.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the solitary sonneteer and the nature lyric
literary_identity: Poet; the most original American sonneteer of the nineteenth century and the great neglected poet of the New England woods.
biography: Born in Boston on 4 February 1821; he graduated from Harvard, studied law, and retired to Greenfield, Massachusetts, after the death of his wife, where he wrote the sonnets and lyrics collected in Poems (1860). He published little and died at Greenfield on 9 May 1873.
literary_profile: Tuckerman wrote the finest American sonnet sequence of the nineteenth century and was the most original nature poet of his generation: his Poems of 1860, largely ignored in his lifetime, were rediscovered in the twentieth century as a central text of American poetry, and his influence runs through Yvor Winters, Robert Frost and the American formal lyric.
stylistic_characteristics: The sonnet sequence on nature and grief; the minute observation of the New England woodland; the harsh, knotted syntax; the elegiac address to the dead wife; the refusal of the popular and the sentimental.
intellectual_concerns: Bereavement and the immortality of the dead; nature as the language of grief; solitude and the woods; the failure of fame; the relation of the poet to the community.
historical_significance: Frederick Goddard Tuckerman was the most original American sonneteer of the nineteenth century: his Poems of 1860, neglected in his lifetime, were rediscovered as a central text of American poetry and his influence runs through Frost and the American formal lyric.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the island poet and the nature sketch
literary_identity: Poet and prose writer; the poet of the Isles of Shoals and one of the finest American nature writers of the century.
biography: Born Celia Laighton in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, on 29 June 1835; she grew up on White Island and then Appledore in the Isles of Shoals, where her father kept the lighthouse and later a hotel. Poems (1872), Among the Isles of Shoals (1873), Drift-Weed (1878) and An Island Garden (1894) followed. She died at the Isles of Shoals on 26 August 1894.
literary_profile: Celia Thaxter was the poet of the Isles of Shoals and one of the finest American nature writers of the nineteenth century: Among the Isles of Shoals and An Island Garden created the island memoir, and her poems of the sea and the garden made the New England coast into a literary landscape.
stylistic_characteristics: The island lyric of the sea and the weather; the prose sketch of the shore and the garden; the close observation of the natural world; the plain quatrain of the popular poet; the record of the seasonal round.
intellectual_concerns: The sea and the island; the garden and the cultivation of the ground; childhood and the lighthouse home; solitude and the natural world; the seasonal cycle and mortality.
historical_significance: Celia Thaxter was the poet of the Isles of Shoals and one of the finest American nature writers of the century: Among the Isles of Shoals and An Island Garden created the island memoir and made the New England coast a literary landscape.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the newspaper sketch and the woman's voice
literary_identity: Columnist and novelist; the highest-paid newspaper writer in the United States in the 1850s and the author of Ruth Hall.
biography: Born Sara Payson Willis in Portland, Maine, on 12 July 1811; widowed with two children, she began writing for the Boston newspapers under the name Fanny Fern in 1851 and became the highest-paid columnist in the country, writing for the New York Ledger. Fern Leaves from Fanny's Portfolio (1853) and Ruth Hall (1855) followed, and she died in New York on 10 October 1872.
literary_profile: Fanny Fern was the highest-paid newspaper writer in the United States in the 1850s and the first American woman to make a fortune from the personal column. Ruth Hall is the first American novel of a woman's professional independence, and her sketches created the American newspaper column as a woman's form.
stylistic_characteristics: The short newspaper sketch in the first person; the direct address to the reader; the comic exaggeration and the sudden pathos; the domestic detail turned into argument; the sententious closing line.
intellectual_concerns: The woman question and the limited estate; poverty and the professional woman writer; the family and its hypocrisies; the metropolis and the new market for print; marriage and widowhood.
historical_significance: Fanny Fern was the highest-paid newspaper writer in America in the 1850s and the first woman to make a fortune from the personal column: Ruth Hall is the first American novel of a woman's professional independence, and her sketches created the newspaper column as a woman's form.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the ornamental tale and the New England romance
literary_identity: Short-story writer, poet and novelist; the most brilliant of the American magazine story-writers of the 1860s.
biography: Born Harriet Elizabeth Prescott in Calais, Maine, on 3 April 1835; she was educated at the Pinkerton Academy and made her name with 'In a Cellar' in the Atlantic Monthly in 1859. The Amber Gods and Other Stories (1863) followed, and she wrote steadily for the magazines for the rest of her life. She married Richard Spofford in 1865 and died at Deer Island, Massachusetts, on 14 August 1921.
literary_profile: Harriet Prescott Spofford was the most brilliant of the American magazine story-writers of the 1860s and one of the finest prose stylists of the American nineteenth century: The Amber Gods created the ornamental, sensuous American tale, and her Gothic stories of New England brought the decadent style into American fiction.
stylistic_characteristics: The ornate, jewelled prose of the magazine tale; the Gothic situation in a New England setting; the sensuous description and the delayed revelation; the supernatural explained and unexplained; the frame narrative.
intellectual_concerns: Art versus life and the romance of the artist; the supernatural and the haunted house; the position of women in marriage; the New England past and its secrets; death and the beautiful corpse.
historical_significance: Harriet Prescott Spofford was the most brilliant of the American magazine story-writers of the 1860s: The Amber Gods created the ornamental American tale, brought the decadent style into American fiction, and made her the finest prose stylist of her generation after Hawthorne.
